--- title: "Einführung in R und Quarto" subtitle: "Data Frames & Tibbles" author: "Andreas Haupt" bibliography: IntRo.bib format: revealjs: theme: style.scss css: global.css slideNumber: true fig-align: center editor: source execute: echo: false message: false warning: false --- ## Some vectors ::: {.cell} ::: ```r # Now create a couple of vectors, similar to # the variables in the ALLBUS gender data. (age <- c(52, 51, 32, 60, 76)) (sex <- factor(x = c("Mann", "Frau", "Frau", "Frau", "Frau"), levels = c("Mann", "Frau", "Divers"))) (eastwest <- factor(x = c("West", "West", "Ost", "West", "West"), levels = c("West", "Ost"))) (incc <- c(2000, 1800, 950, 1300, 1300)) (id03 <- c(6, 6, 6, 5, 8)) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 52 51 32 60 76 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Mann Frau Frau Frau Frau Levels: Mann Frau Divers ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] West West Ost West West Levels: West Ost ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2000 1800 950 1300 1300 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 6 6 5 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Data frames **Data frames** organize vectors of *equal length* along their indices. ```r # Bind our 5 vectors along their index into a data frame. # Assign that data frame to object "Dat". (Dat <- data.frame(sex, age, eastwest, incc, id03)) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sex age eastwest incc id03 1 Mann 52 West 2000 6 2 Frau 51 West 1800 6 3 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 4 Frau 60 West 1300 5 5 Frau 76 West 1300 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Tibbles **Tibbles** are data frames. But they have some improved features, so we will work with them. ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ```r # As a comparison, print the former(!) # data frame Dat. Dat ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sex age eastwest incc id03 1 Mann 52 West 2000 6 2 Frau 51 West 1800 6 3 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 4 Frau 60 West 1300 5 5 Frau 76 West 1300 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ```r # Make Dat a tibble and assign it to object "Dat", # (effectively overwriting Dat as a tibble). (Dat <- as_tibble(Dat)) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 sex age eastwest incc id03 1 Mann 52 West 2000 6 2 Frau 51 West 1800 6 3 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 4 Frau 60 West 1300 5 5 Frau 76 West 1300 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Address single variables (The `$` operator) ```r # Return variable "eastwest" contained in tibble Dat. # (R for Data Science mentions two further commands.) Dat$eastwest ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] West West Ost West West Levels: West Ost ``` ::: ::: ::: ```r # Give a summary of numeric vector age contained in Dat. summary(Dat$age) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 32.0 51.0 52.0 54.2 60.0 76.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ```r # Give a summary of factor vector sex contained in Dat. summary(Dat$sex) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mann Frau Divers 1 4 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `select()` several variables ```r # Select from tibble Dat the variables sex and id03, # and assign them to the new object Dat_small. (Dat_small <- select(Dat, sex, id03)) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 sex id03 1 Mann 6 2 Frau 6 3 Frau 6 4 Frau 5 5 Frau 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `select()` several variables `select()` has a couple of nice **helper functions**, see `?select` for details. ```r # Select from object Dat all variables that start with i, # and assign the result to a new object Dat_small. (Dat_small <- select(Dat, starts_with("i"))) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 incc id03 1 2000 6 2 1800 6 3 950 6 4 1300 5 5 1300 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `filter()` cases (Based on values in certain variables) ```r # Either, use dplyr's (part of tidyverse) filter() function, # to return all cases contained in Dat living in Ost. (Dat_small <- dplyr::filter(Dat, eastwest == "Ost")) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 sex age eastwest incc id03 1 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: . . . ```r # Or use the index, to achieve the same. (Dat_small <- Dat[Dat$eastwest == "Ost", ]) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 sex age eastwest incc id03 1 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.centered} Why is there a `,` after `"Ost"`? ::: ## Index (Rows, and columns) In contrast to vectors, data frames and tibbles have rows and columns. As in matrix algebra, R's index thus distinguishes `[rows, columns]`. The `,` after `"Ost"` tells R that we talk about rows. To understand how the index method works, remember logical vectors: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ```r # Print factor eastwest contained in tibble Dat. Dat$eastwest # Return a logical vector of whether the different # elements in Dat$eastwest equal "Ost". Dat$eastwest == "Ost" # Feed the logical vector to the index of Dat # to select TRUE cases living in Ost. (Dat_small <- Dat[Dat$eastwest == "Ost", ]) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] West West Ost West West Levels: West Ost ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 sex age eastwest incc id03 1 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} . . . ```r # Create a new logical variable called "selector", # which identifies cases living in Ost in Dat$eastwest. Dat$selector <- Dat$eastwest == "Ost" # Print Dat. Dat ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 6 sex age eastwest incc id03 selector 1 Mann 52 West 2000 6 FALSE 2 Frau 51 West 1800 6 FALSE 3 Frau 32 Ost 950 6 TRUE 4 Frau 60 West 1300 5 FALSE 5 Frau 76 West 1300 8 FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Transform, recode & generate (Variables of tibbles) To transform and recode simply use `$` to clarify which tibble you are referring to. ```r # Center age around the average age. (Dat$age <- Dat$age - mean(Dat$age)) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -2.2 -3.2 -22.2 5.8 21.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ```r # Recode "Ost" to "Neue Bundeslaender". (Dat$eastwest <- fct_recode(Dat$eastwest, "Neue Bundeslaender" = "Ost")) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] West West Neue Bundeslaender West [5] West Levels: West Neue Bundeslaender ``` ::: ::: ::: If you rather want to generate a new variable, just give it a name. ```r # Devide age by its standard deviation; # now it is z-standardized (mean = 0, sd = 1). (Dat$z_age <- Dat$age / sd(Dat$age)) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.1379860 -0.2007069 -1.3924038 0.3637812 1.3673154 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Transform, recode & generate (Several variables of a tibble) If you want to transform and recode several variables from the same tibble, get used to use `mutate()`. ::: {.note} You will better understand why in Session 6 on piping! ::: ```r (Dat <- mutate(Dat, # Use the Dat tibble. incc = incc - mean(incc), # Transform to deviation from average. z_incc = incc / sd(incc), # z-standardize incc. eastwest = fct_recode(eastwest, # Recode eastwest. "Alte Bundeslaender" = "West", # "West" to "Alte Bundeslaender". "Neue Bundeslaender" = "Ost") # "Ost" to "Neue Bundeslaender". ) # Don't forget to close mutate's bracket ")" ) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 sex age eastwest incc id03 selector z_age z_incc 1 Mann -2.20 Alte Bundeslaender 530 6 FALSE -0.138 1.25 2 Frau -3.20 Alte Bundeslaender 330 6 FALSE -0.201 0.779 3 Frau -22.2 Neue Bundeslaender -520 6 TRUE -1.39 -1.23 4 Frau 5.8 Alte Bundeslaender -170 5 FALSE 0.364 -0.401 5 Frau 21.8 Alte Bundeslaender -170 8 FALSE 1.37 -0.401 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.note} Also, look how RStudio structures the brackets. It helps you to understand, within which function things are happening. ::: ## Conditional transform & recode ((i.e., for filtered cases)) To transform/recode only among certain cases, use `case_when()`. ```r (Dat <- mutate( Dat, # Mutate variables contained in Dat. sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex, eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers", age < 0 & id03 < 1 ~ "Keine Angabe", # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe", TRUE ~ as.character(sex) # 3. and all others ~ leave as is; ) # close case_when's bracket. )) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 sex age eastwest incc id03 selector z_age z_incc 1 Mann -2.20 Alte Bundeslaender 530 6 FALSE -0.138 1.25 2 Frau -3.20 Alte Bundeslaender 330 6 FALSE -0.201 0.779 3 Divers -22.2 Neue Bundeslaender -520 6 TRUE -1.39 -1.23 4 Frau 5.8 Alte Bundeslaender -170 5 FALSE 0.364 -0.401 5 Frau 21.8 Alte Bundeslaender -170 8 FALSE 1.37 -0.401 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Conditional transform & recode ((i.e., for filtered cases)) ::: {.cell} ::: The three lines of this `case_when()` application do the following thing: 1. For all cases from the Neue Bundeslaender with a below-average income ~ recode sex to "Divers". 2. For all those who're younger than 0 and score below 1 on the Oben-Unten-Skala ~ recode sex to "Keine Angabe". 3. All remaining cases ~ use their original sex values, but transform them to a character vector. - Remember, R is class sensitive! It will not combine numeric information into a character vector. Because we give `case_when()` `"Divers"` and `"Keine Angabe"` as new values, it assumes that we want to make sex a character vector. Thus we cannot supply the former factor values (which are integer) in line three. ## `case_when()` and `NA` ```r (Dat <- mutate( Dat, sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex, eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers", age < 0 & id03 < 1 ~ "Keine Angabe", # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe", TRUE ~ NA_real_ # 3. and all others ~ NA ) # close case_when's bracket. )) ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `mutate()`: ℹ In argument: `sex = case_when(...)`. Caused by error in `case_when()`: ! Can't combine `..1 (right)` and `..3 (right)` . ``` ::: ::: ::: In R vectors are type sensitive; the elements of one vector may only be of one type. Because we give `case_when()` `"Divers"` and `"Keine Angabe"` as new values, it wants to make sex a character vector. But `NA` is a *logical* constant, and `NA_real_` a *numeric* one — neither combines with character values. If you type `?NA`, you will learn: > "*NA is a logical* constant of length 1 which contains a missing value indicator. *NA can be coerced to any other vector type* except raw." ## `case_when()` and `NA` `NA` are type sensitive, too! Therefore, coerce NA to character/numeric with `as.character()`/`as.numeric()`. ```r (Dat <- mutate( Dat, sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex, eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers", age < 0 & id03 < 1 ~ "Keine Angabe", # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe", TRUE ~ as.character(NA) # 3. and all others ~ NA ) # close case_when's bracket. )) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket. ``` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 sex age eastwest incc id03 selector z_age z_incc 1 -2.20 Alte Bundeslaender 530 6 FALSE -0.138 1.25 2 -3.20 Alte Bundeslaender 330 6 FALSE -0.201 0.779 3 Divers -22.2 Neue Bundeslaender -520 6 TRUE -1.39 -1.23 4 5.8 Alte Bundeslaender -170 5 FALSE 0.364 -0.401 5 21.8 Alte Bundeslaender -170 8 FALSE 1.37 -0.401 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.note} Alternatively, you can also use type-specific `NA`: `NA_character_`, `NA_real_`, etc.. ::: ## Import downloaded data The classic way to work with actual data, is to download them to some folder and to then import them to your software environment. The tidyverse contains the following three packages: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://haven.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="30%"} - The "haven" package allows you to import Stata, SPSS, and SAS files. ::: {.note} See the respective [Haven Website](https://haven.tidyverse.org/). ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://readr.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="65%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="65%"} ::: ::: - The "readr" package allows you to import csv, tsv and fwf files.
::: {.note} See the respective [Readr Website](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) and [Cheat Sheet](https://rawgit.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/master/data-import.pdf). ::: - The readxl package allows you to read in Excel's xlsx files. ::: {.note} See the respective [Readxl Website](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/). ::: ::: ::: ## First steps with the genderdata ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} . . . ::: {.centered} Not very telling...
But remember, R does not do labels,
in contrast to Stata or SPSS! ::: ![](https://i.vimeocdn.com/portrait/3399477_300x300){width="40%"} ::: ::: ## Importing labelled data! ::: {.column width="50%"} R imports Stata and SPSS labels, but cannot handle them. Thus, when you import Stata or SPSS data,
... you need to change each labelled variable to **numeric or factor** from the outset of your analysis!! ::: ## Importing labelled data! ::: {.column width="50%"} If you want to use a variable as categorical, use `as_factor()` to make the labels the new factor levels: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ## Importing labelled data! ::: {.column width="50%"} If you want to use a variable as numeric, use `zap_labels()` to prohibit problems with the imported labels: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: --- ## Today's general lessons 1. *Data frames* organize equally-sized vectors along their indices; *Tibbles* are modernized data frames. The indices of data frames/tibbles are organized as `[row, column]`. 2. *Helper functions* are sub-functions that help you to make coding easier in many ways. They only work within the confines of the function for which they were designed as helpers. 3. Addressing variables means to address the columns of a data frame. Filtering cases means to address certain rows. Both is possible via the index `[row, column]`, but the `filter()` and `select()` functions have advantages. 4. R has no labels. The idea is that numeric variables have a scale (e.g., cm, years, DKK), while categorical variables have no true representation in numbers. When you import labelled data from Stata or SPSS, the labels are stored in R but will create confusion in the mid run. Make sure to `zap_labels()` from numeric variables and to treat categorical variables `as_factor()`. ## Today's important operators 1. `$`: Allows your to address vectors contained in a data frame/tibble. ## Today's (important) functions 1. `data.frame()`: organize several vectors of equal length by their index. 2. `as_tibble()`: take a data frame and make it a Tibble. 3. `read_rds()`: import an R data file (.rds) into your session. 4. `summary()`: Give a summary of an object. 5. `select()`: select several variables from a data frame/Tibble. 6. `filter()`: filter cases based on values in certain variables. 7. `mutate()`: Adds new variables and preserves existing. Good for recoding several variables. 8. `case_when()`: Conditional recode for cases filtered in complex ways. 9. `as_factor()`: Make a labelled Stata/SPSS variable a factor. 10. `zap_labels()`: Make a labelled Stata/SPSS variable numeric. ## Literatur ::: {#refs} :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
